source.title: Learning in PINNs: Phase transition, diffusion equilibrium, and generalization
source.authors: Sokratis J. Anagnostopoulos; Juan Diego Toscano; Nikolaos Stergiopulos; G. Karniadakis

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices and references.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own PINN training results, but studies PDE solution accuracy and generalization rather than classification training error or any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper's PINNs are trained with Adam on PDE and data residual losses. Its reported outcomes concern relative L2 test error, residual homogeneity, and gradient SNR, not classification training error. Rows record explicit PINN outcomes as findings about adjacent neural-network training behavior.
record.test_reason: The study measures PINN solution error, residual homogeneity and gradient SNR under residual-based attention (RBA). It does not test any listed version. Its proposed connection to edge-of-stability training is speculative: it measures neither Hessian sharpness nor a learning-rate stability threshold.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors identify fitting, diffusion and diffusion-equilibrium phases in their PINN experiments and associate gradient alignment plus residual homogeneity with faster convergence and better generalization. RBA often improves these outcomes, with Burgers an exception. Generality beyond PINNs remains untested, and the connection to edge-of-stability training is an interpretation rather than a measured result.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses full-batch Adam for PINNs with PDE residual and boundary/data losses, and compares vanilla training with residual-based attention weighting. It does not use the classification-training recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Benchmark and residual structure affect outcomes: RBA performs worse on Burgers because its weights focus on an unresolved discontinuity; the cerebral-flow case has a brief DE phase.

fits_no_version.finding: RBA reaches 10% Allen-Cahn test error in 10k rather than 100k iterations and reduces cavity-flow final test error from approximately 60% to 6%. Cerebral-flow improvements are qualitative. RBA performs slightly worse on Burgers, attributed to weighting an unresolved steep region.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual-based weighting can accelerate PINN solution convergence and improve test accuracy, with benefits depending on the PDE and residual structure.

fits_no_version.finding: A rise and stabilization in gradient SNR accompanies improved solution convergence. Appendix A's batch-size-adjusted SNR remains slightly below one during equilibrium. These measurements do not establish edge-of-stability sharpness dynamics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: PINN convergence can coincide with a transition toward greater sample-gradient alignment and residual homogeneity.

record.problems: No parametric investigation of architecture or hyperparameters; the authors defer that work. Results are PINN-specific examples and do not establish classification training-error outcomes. Several test-error comparisons are qualitative or approximate, with no uncertainty estimates stated.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified outcomes were reported in text for Helmholtz or other cerebral-flow comparisons beyond the aggregate statements retained in R8; plots are described qualitatively and precise figure values are not extracted.

untested.parts: CIFAR classification training error, random or corrupted labels, and effects of model size, stopping and regularization.
ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious-minimum frequencies and extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation, identity shortcuts, special initialization and normalization-free residual training.
Initialization comparisons, signal and gradient propagation at initialization, training speed and trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, initial loss growth, curvature reduction, sharpness hovering near the threshold and divergence conditions.
Batch-normalization comparisons, learning-rate tolerance and Fixup. The cerebral-flow use of weight normalization has no corresponding ablation and does not test batch normalization.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are relative to the supplied claim versions; cannot_determine does not dispute the reported PINN comparisons. These comparisons belong under fits_no_version rather than serving as evidence for V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100 classification training error; random or corrupted labels; model size, optimizer, regularization, and stopping conditions.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima frequency, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual CNN depth and training error; shortcut effects; special initialization or normalization-free residual training.
Activation-matched or orthogonal initialization effects on training speed and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss/curvature dynamics, and edge-of-stability behavior in the stated settings.
Batch normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

rows.value: Converges to a stationary solution with high test error due to heterogeneous residual regions

rows.check: The qualitative stationary-solution finding is supported but bears on no version. Appendix D specifies ordered mini-batches for PDE and boundary points, full-data PTV updates, and weight normalization; this case should not be described as uniformly full-batch training.

rows.baseline: vanilla model converges to a stationary solution with high test error
rows.value: RBA resolves the high-residual regions; the paper says RBA models show about one order of magnitude faster convergence overall
rows.note: No numeric test-error value is given for the cerebral case; the speed statement is an aggregate across the cases.
rows.check: Separate the qualitative cerebral-flow result from the aggregate claim of approximately tenfold faster convergence; the latter is not a cerebral-specific measurement. Include the ordered-mini-batch and weight-normalization conditions from Appendix D. Neither result tests a listed version.
